client: I started a new job in marketing about a month ago, and honestly, it's been really rough. Everyone around me seems so confident and experienced, and I just feel like I'm constantly falling behind no matter how hard I try. I'm not even sure talking about it will change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a quiet but persistent heaviness right now — not panic, but that draining sense of just never quite feeling like you're keeping up, which can be really exhausting in its own way. I'm really glad you decided to give this a shot, and I want you to know that what you're feeling is incredibly common when stepping into a new environment, even if it doesn't make it any less hard. I'm curious — when you notice yourself feeling behind, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in those moments?

client: Honestly, the thoughts that come up are pretty harsh. It's mostly stuff like "everyone can see you don't belong here" or "you're going to get found out eventually." It's like there's this constant voice in my head waiting for the moment someone finally realizes they made a mistake hiring me.
therapist: What you're describing — that waiting-to-be-found-out feeling — actually has a name: it's called impostor syndrome, and it's remarkably common among people who are actually quite capable, which tells us something important about those harsh thoughts. In CBT, we'd call those kinds of thoughts "cognitive distortions" — they feel very true and certain, but they're not necessarily accurate reflections of reality. I'm wondering, in your first month, has there been even one small moment where you did something well, or where someone responded positively to your work?

client: I mean, yeah, there was one moment where my manager said my copy for a campaign was "a good start" and asked me to build on it. But honestly, my brain just kind of dismissed that — like, "good start" isn't exactly glowing praise, and maybe she was just being nice. I hear what you're saying about impostor syndrome, but knowing there's a name for it doesn't really make the feeling go away, you know?
therapist: You're absolutely right that naming something doesn't magically dissolve the feeling, and I appreciate you pushing back on that — that's actually really important self-awareness. What I find interesting though is what your mind just did with that feedback: your manager gave you a concrete, actionable response to your work, and your brain almost instantly rewrote it as either meaningless or fake — that's the impostor syndrome doing its job, filtering out evidence that doesn't fit the story of "I don't belong here." What do you think it would take for a piece of positive feedback to actually feel believable to you?

client: That's a hard question, honestly. I think part of me feels like I'd need something really undeniable — like, multiple people consistently saying I'm doing great over a long period of time — before I'd actually believe it. But even as I say that, I kind of realize that bar is almost impossible to reach, which is a frustrating thing to notice about myself.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in what you just did — you caught yourself setting an almost unreachable standard and recognized it as unfair, which takes genuine self-awareness and honesty. That bar you described — needing overwhelming, sustained proof before believing you're doing okay — is worth examining, because it essentially guarantees the critical voice always wins, no matter what actually happens around you. Where do you think that standard comes from — is this a pattern that shows up in other areas of your life too, or does it feel specific to this job?

client: Honestly, I think it shows up pretty much everywhere. Like, in friendships too — I often feel like I need to prove I'm worth someone's time before I can really relax around them, otherwise I'm just waiting for them to realize I'm not that interesting or valuable. I guess I never really connected those two things before, but saying it out loud now it does feel like the same pattern, which is kind of unsettling to sit with.
therapist: It makes sense that this feels unsettling to sit with — you've just made a really significant connection, and realizing a pattern runs deeper than you thought can feel both clarifying and a little daunting at the same time. What you're describing sounds like a core belief about your own worth — almost like a rule you've been living by that says "I have to earn my place, always," and that kind of belief tends to quietly shape so much of how we experience the world without us even realizing it. I'm curious — when you think back, do you have any sense of where that rule might have first taken root for you?

client: I think it probably goes back to growing up — my parents weren't neglectful or anything, but praise was pretty rare, and it felt like you had to really achieve something significant to get acknowledgment. So I think I just internalized this idea that baseline you aren't quite enough, and you have to keep demonstrating your value. It's weird to say that out loud because I don't want to blame them, and I'm not even sure digging into all of that will actually help me feel less anxious at work on Monday morning.
therapist: It's really thoughtful that you're holding space for your parents while also being honest about how that environment shaped you — those two things can both be true at once, and noticing that takes a lot of maturity. And your concern about Monday morning is completely valid — understanding where a belief comes from doesn't automatically quiet it, but it does give us something to work with, because once we can see the rule clearly ("I'm not enough by default"), we can start to gently challenge it with real evidence rather than just being swept along by it. So thinking practically about Monday — if that voice shows up and says "you don't belong here," what might it look like to talk back to it with even one small piece of evidence from your first month?

client: I guess I could try to remind myself of that campaign feedback, or the fact that I've managed to figure out the workflow tools faster than I expected to. But honestly, in the moment when the anxiety is really spiking, I'm not sure I'll actually have the presence of mind to do that — it feels a bit like being told to do breathing exercises during a panic attack, like the advice makes sense in theory but the execution is a whole other thing. I want to try, I just don't want to set myself up to feel like I've failed at therapy homework too if it doesn't work perfectly.
therapist: That's such an honest and valid concern, and I really don't want this to become another place where you feel like you have to perform perfectly — that would just be the same old pattern showing up in a new room. You're right that in the thick of anxiety, reaching for rational thoughts can feel nearly impossible, so instead of framing this as homework you can pass or fail, what if we thought of it as just noticing — when the voice shows up on Monday, simply observing "there's that pattern again" without any pressure to immediately fix or counter it. Does that feel like a slightly more manageable starting point?

client: Yeah, that actually does feel a bit more manageable — just noticing, without having to fix it on the spot. I think I can probably do that, or at least try to. I guess my only worry is that noticing it might just make me more aware of how often it happens, and I'm not sure if that's going to feel discouraging rather than helpful.
therapist: That's a really thoughtful concern, and it's actually a sign that you're thinking about this carefully rather than just agreeing to feel better in the moment. It's true that noticing the pattern more clearly can initially feel a bit like turning on a light in a messy room — things might seem worse before they feel better, but the mess was always there, and seeing it is the first step to doing something about it. Over time, that same noticing tends to shift from feeling discouraging to feeling like a small moment of power — like you're watching the pattern rather than being completely inside it — but I'm curious, how are you feeling about everything you've uncovered today, sitting with it all right now?

client: Honestly, I feel a bit wrung out — like I came in thinking this was just about a new job and somehow we ended up somewhere much deeper than I expected. There's a part of me that feels a little relieved to have said some of this out loud, but another part that's wondering if I just opened a door I'm not sure I'm ready to walk through. I think I need some time to sit with all of this before I know how I really feel about it.
therapist: What you're feeling right now — that mix of relief and "what did I just open up" — is actually a really healthy and honest response to doing meaningful work, and I want you to honor that rather than push through it. You don't have to walk through that door all at once, and there's no rush — what you've uncovered today will still be there when you're ready, and even just naming these patterns out loud is genuinely significant progress. Be gentle with yourself this week, and I hope you'll come back when you're ready — you've shown a lot of courage today.

client: Thank you, that actually means something to hear — though I notice part of me wants to dismiss even that, which I guess is pretty on brand at this point. I think I will come back, even though I'm still not entirely sure how much this will help with the day-to-day anxiety at work. I just hope next time we can get a bit more into the practical side of things, because I think I need both — understanding the deeper stuff and also having something concrete to hold onto when Monday morning hits.
therapist: I love that you caught yourself dismissing the acknowledgment in real time — that's actually the noticing skill already working, which is worth recognizing. And your ask for next time is completely reasonable and important — understanding the roots of a pattern and having practical tools for Monday morning aren't in tension, they work together, and we'll make sure to build that concrete toolkit alongside the deeper work. I'm really glad you're coming back, and I think you'll find that the two pieces start to reinforce each other more than you might expect right now.
